thread.title: Goldman Sachs Downgrades Apple on iPhone Sales Projection

author: Zehong (Marco) Zhou
title: Goldman Sachs Downgrades Apple on iPhone Sales Projection
text:
11/20/2018 1765
Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) downgraded Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) on Tuesday due to its weaker demand outlook for Apple products especially for its iPhone XR, according to CNBC . Apple shares fell by 3.45% shortly after the opening bell on Tuesday.
Goldman Sachs reiterated its neutral rating on Apple and cut its price target down from USD 209 to USD 182 per share, representing a 2% downside over the next year.
“In addition to weakness in demand for Apple’s products in China and other emerging markets it also looks like the balance of price and features in the iPhone XR may not have been well-received,” Goldman analyst Rod Hall wrote Tuesday.
“Our estimates remain at the lower end of Apple’s guidance range at this point as we believe the company likely included this more negative scenario in its provided range,” Hall added.
Goldman Sachs now sees Apple’s earnings per year for fiscal 2019 at USD 13.40, approximately in-line with Apple’s last three years next-twelve month average.
In September, Apple released three new iPhone models: iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max and the iPhone XR. Recently, the Company cut its production orders for all three iPhones, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.
Last week, Apple’s supplier, Lumentum, released a quarterly report in which it did not provide a sales forecast for Apple. Apple accounts for approximately 30% of Lumentum’s revenue. The undisclosed guidance led investors and analysts to believe that iPhone demand is declining.
Apple also announced earlier this month that it would not release individual sales numbers for its iPhone, iPad and Mac. The three products will be streamlined into one revenue figure on the Company’s quarterly financial results.
Apple’s decision to combine the three products’ revenue numbers shows that iPhone sales may be slowing down in the future. Goldman Sachs said that Apple is combated the slowed iPhone sales by raising its prices.
“Apple’s success with iPhone X demand this summer and then a relatively healthy start to the XS cycle this fall suggested to us that pricing power was still intact,” Hall wrote. “However, the laboratory of the market now points to Apple being at the limit of their price premium for the iPhone. In our experience with mobile phones, when pricing power is lost, consumer technology companies tend to either lose margins or market share or both.”
